title: State of the Claw — Peter Steinberger
talk_summary: Peter Steinberger recounts running OpenClaw: massive agent-driven security-report volume (1,142 advisories, ~16.6/day), most being AI-generated 'slop', and describes his coding workflow of running ~5-6 parallel agent sessions, iterating rather than waterfall, and treating 'taste' and system design as the human bottleneck. The talk is mostly project narrative and security-industry commentary, but a few mechanisms (parallel agent sessions, plugin-based extensibility, trust/reputation tiers, memory 'dreaming', saying no to scope) are transferable.

takeaways.technique: Parallel agent sessions as a throughput workaround
takeaways.what_they_do: Runs multiple concurrent agent sessions (previously ~10, now ~5-6) because each loop is slow; treats concurrency as a temporary workaround until models get faster.
takeaways.evidence_quote: there's times where I was running almost 10 sessions at the same time

takeaways.technique: Triage AI-generated reports by plausibility, not severity label
takeaways.what_they_do: Treats high-severity security reports skeptically because most are AI-generated slop; uses human judgment to filter before acting, and warns that rushed fixes break the product.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the higher they screaming how critical they are, the more likely it's slop

takeaways.technique: Human 'taste' as the merge gate, not full automation
takeaways.what_they_do: Rejects fully automated PR merging because AI can't judge product direction; keeps a vision document and human taste as the bottleneck even with heavy agent use.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you don't just want to build a pipeline that just merges PRs because a lot of them just don't make sense

takeaways.technique: Dreaming / memory reconciliation over session logs
takeaways.what_they_do: Runs a periodic 'dream' pass that garbage-collects session logs, promoting some memories to long-term storage and dropping others, analogous to human sleep consolidation.
Refactored a spaghetti codebase so everything (memory, wiki, dreaming) is a replaceable plugin, letting users extend without PRs to core.
takeaways.evidence_quote: everything is an extension a plug-in. So you can replace memory, you can add the wicki

takeaways.technique: Saying no as a scoping discipline
takeaways.what_they_do: Treats 'saying no' as a core skill because any idea is one prompt away, and the problem is how many ideas fit together, not any single one.
takeaways.evidence_quote: a skill that is becoming more and more important is saying no
